{{short description|Giant panda expert and Chinese conservationist (born 1965)}}
{{family name hatnote|[[Lü (surname)|Lü]]|lang=Chinese}}

'''Lü Zhi''' ({{zh|s=吕植|p=Lǚ Zhí}}; born 1965) is a Chinese conservation biologist, [[Giant panda|panda]] expert and an expert on [[biodiversity]]. She is a professor at [[Peking University]] and also the executive director of the Peking University Center for Nature and Society.<ref name=":0">{{Cite web|url = http://www.nationalgeographic.com/explorers/grants-programs/gef/china/lu-zhi/|title = Lü Zhi|access-date = 20 November 2015|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20180309121751/https://www.nationalgeographic.com/explorers/grants-programs/gef/china/lu-zhi/|archive-date=2018-03-09|website = National Geographic Explorers|publisher = National Geographic}}</ref> Lü is also the founder of the Shanshui Conservation Center which is dedicated to preserving the Three Rivers Headwater Region in [[Yushu Tibetan Autonomous Prefecture|Yushu]], [[Qinghai]].<ref>{{Cite news|url = http://www.huffingtonpost.com/the-groundtruth-project/climate-change-rears-its_b_8491232.html|title = Climate Change Rears Its Head on the Tibetan Plateau|last = Feng|first = Coco|date = 6 January 2015|work = Huffington Post|access-date = 21 November 2015}}</ref>

== Biography ==
Lü began studying at Peking University in 1981, when she was sixteen.<ref name=":1">{{Cite news|url = http://www.womenofchina.cn/womenofchina/html1/people/everyday/7/7109-1.htm|title = Lu Zhi: Pandas Are Her Thing|date = 14 April 2006|work = Women of China|access-date = 20 November 2015}}</ref> By 1992, she had completed all of her undergraduate and post-doctorate work at the same university.<ref name=":1" /> Her work with giant pandas began when she was nineteen, when she became part of a long-term [[Field research|field study]] on the animals, their [[habitat]] and their [[genetic diversity]].<ref name=":1" /> During her field work, she created bonds with some of the pandas, helped a sick panda eat again and also became one of the first people to go inside of a wild panda's den.<ref name=":1" /> She also taught herself the skill of wildlife-photography while in the field, and her pictures were featured in ''[[National Geographic (magazine)|National Geographic]]'' in 1993 and 1995.<ref>{{Cite book|title = Tears of the Cheetah: The Genetic Secrets of Our Animal Ancestors|last = O'Brien|first = Stephen J.|publisher = Thomas Dunne Books|year = 2003|isbn = 0312272863|location = New York|pages = [https://archive.org/details/tearsofcheetah00step/page/148 148–151]|url-access = registration|url = https://archive.org/details/tearsofcheetah00step/page/148}}</ref>

From 1995 to 2000, she worked as a program office for the [[World Wide Fund for Nature|World Wildlife Fund]] (WWF) China.<ref name=":2">{{Cite web|url = http://www.weforum.org/global-agenda-councils/lu-zhi|title = Lu Zhi|access-date = 20 November 2015|website = World Economic Forum}}</ref> At WWF, she developed programs and activities which focused on the giant panda and also on the [[Tibet Autonomous Region|Tibetan Autonomous Region]].<ref name=":1" /> She also helped to open the WWF Tibet office and to raise the total annual budget for conservation focusing on the panda and Tibet.<ref name=":1" /> In 2002, she began to work at [[Conservation International]] (CI).<ref name=":2" /> Lü Zhi worked as the head of CI's China office.<ref name=":3">{{Cite news|url = http://china.blogs.nytimes.com/2007/08/30/questions-for-lu-zhi/?_r=0|title = China and The Environment: Answers from Lu Zhi|date = 30 August 2007|work = The New York Times|access-date = 20 November 2015}}</ref>

Lü's [[Conservation biology|conservation]] work focuses on several large endangered species, including the giant panda, [[snow leopard]], [[Przewalski's gazelle]] and the Tibetan brown bear.<ref name=":0" /> Her non-governmental organization (NGO), the Shanshui Conservation Center was founded in 2007 in order to help develop "community-based, [[Grassroots democracy|grassroots]] solutions to conservation in western China."<ref>{{Cite web|url = http://www.rolexawards.com/profiles/jury/zhi_lu|title = Lu Zhi: 2014 Jury Member|access-date = 20 November 2015|website = Rolex Awards for Enterprise|publisher = Rolex}}</ref> She emphasizes the importance of community-managed nature reserves in the fight to protect species and habitats, saying that these types of models are of benefit to both animals and sustainable use of the land by people.<ref>{{Cite journal|url = http://search.ebscohost.com/login.aspx?direct=true&db=a9h&AN=51907177&site=ehost-live|title = Biodiversity Is Life|date = July 2010|journal = Beijing Review|access-date = 20 November 2015|volume = 53|issue = 26|pages = 40–43|url-access=subscription |via=Ebsco}}</ref> Lü Zhi hopes to see a "new economic system that recognises and pays for the value of nature" and at Shan Shui, they model these kinds of economic systems for the larger Chinese government.<ref>{{Cite journal|title = Saving Wild China|last = McKenna|first = Phil|date = 18 July 2009|journal = New Scientist|doi = 10.1016/S0262-4079(09)61895-9|volume = 203|issue = 2717|page = 25 }}</ref> In addition to research and developing community-based conservation efforts, she has also worked with the Chinese government and businesses in order to develop more environmentally-friendly legislation and practices.<ref name=":3" />

Lü has written and co-authored several books about science. Her book, ''Giant Pandas in the Wild'' (2002), was called "a work of art" by ''[[Library Journal]]''.<ref>{{Cite journal|url = http://search.ebscohost.com/login.aspx?direct=true&db=lfh&AN=9634989&site=ehost-live|title = Giant Pandas In The Wild (Book)|last = Emerson|first = Deborah|date = 2003|journal = Library Journal|access-date = 20 November 2015|volume = 128|issue = 8|page = 151|url-access=subscription |via=Ebsco}}</ref>

Additional information
Dr. Lü Zhi, a conservationist from China, graduated from the Department of Biology at Peking University in 1985, marking the beginning of her journey in nature conservation.<ref>{{cite web |title=LÜ ZHI |url=https://www.decadeonrestoration.org/advisory-board/lu-zhi |website=Ecosystem Restoration  |access-date=16 November 2023}}</ref> Since the age of 19, she has demonstrated her interest in studying nature, particularly focusing on research related to giant pandas and endangered animals. She has even spent most of her time living among the pandas, forming friendships with them, and providing care for their illnesses. Through interviews with Dr. Lü's colleagues, it is evident that she is a hardworking, straightforward, and equitable teacher. Even when her students hesitate in the face of difficulties, she criticizes and encourages them to overcome challenges. At the same time, Dr. Lü feels guilty for spending too much time on research and not enough time teaching her students. She also expresses remorse that her conservation efforts are not sufficient to offset human destruction of the environment, yet she continues to strive for environmental protection.<ref>{{cite web |title=Pandas Are Her Thing |url=http://www.china.org.cn/english/environment/148403.htm |website=China Internet Information Center |publisher=China Daily |access-date=16 November 2023}}</ref>
Additionally, she is the founder of the Shanshui Conservation Center and serves as the Vice President of the China Women's Association for Science and Technology. Dr. Lü is known for her pioneering work in community-based conservation and citizen sciences, advocating for coexistence between humans and nature through economic, cultural, and policy initiatives.  She also plays an active role in shaping conservation policy at regional, national, and international levels. 
Furthermore, she has authored numerous articles and books related to conservation and is recognized globally for her contributions. In 2007, she established the Shanshui Conservation Center, focusing on grassroots conservation solutions in western China, and has been involved in significant field projects on various endangered species.  Her research on the giant panda led her to a deeper study of the Sacred Lakes and Mountains in the Tibetan region, providing insights into Tibetan Buddhist conservation practices. In high-altitude forest areas, the climate is extremely cold and the housing conditions are very harsh and rudimentary. At that time, people would not have thought that a woman could overcome difficulties and spend eight years in the wilderness. Many people thought that Lü Zhi was only conducting research on pandas, but in reality, Lü had already developed a strong friendship with the pandas. Lü also took photos with the pandas, documenting their wonderful moments and stories together, which further earned people's respect for this woman. <ref>{{cite web |last1=Shi |first1=Lihong |title=The Science of Sacred Mountain: An Extended Interview with Dr. Lü Zhi |url=https://pulitzercenter.org/stories/science-sacred-mountain-extended-interview-dr-lu-zhi |website=Pulitzer Center |access-date=16 November 2023}}</ref>
After conducting research, Lü Zhi and her classmates published the world's first comprehensive studies of the giant pandas living in the wild in the Qinling Mountains. In their paper, they discussed the significant impact of human activities such as logging and farming on the giant panda's habitat. Fortunately, as a result of this research, logging activities have been halted and China has established a new nature reserve in the Qinling Mountains. It is noteworthy that Lü Zhi and four other women have been awarded the "Chinese Young Women in Science Fellowship," further highlighting the role of women in scientific development. When facing challenges in her research and societal doubts about women's abilities, Dr. Lü expressed, "I am only enjoying what I do."<ref>{{cite web |last1=Li |first1=Xing |title=Environment key to gender equality |url=https://www.chinadaily.com.cn/english/Opinion/2005-11/10/content_493363.htm |website=China Daily |access-date=16 November 2023}}</ref>
